query: More than a century of research on conventional steels and other alloys has shown that exposure within certain temperature ranges can sharply reduce toughness and threaten safety in aerospace, shipping, and petrochemical applications. High-entropy alloys offer attractive strength, ductility, resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement, and wear resistance; however, their multicomponent chemistry complicates predictions of long-term mechanical reliability. Their resistance to rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation does not establish whether their toughness will remain stable after service-relevant heating, and this uncertainty limits engineering use. For a high-performance multicomponent high-entropy alloy in its as-designed condition, under the constraint that its original strength–ductility combination must be retained, what single testable hypothesis proposes an intervention to reduce post-exposure toughness degradation? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to an otherwise identical untreated baseline, define the temperature, duration, and loading boundaries, identify supporting evidence from the observations summarized above, and describe a decisive experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloys can reduce post-exposure toughness degradation through Snoek relaxation
generation.mechanism: Snoek relaxation reduces grain coarsening and intermetallic formation
generation.falsification_experiment: Decisive experiment to falsify the hypothesis

cited_evidence.text: We developed high-temperature high-damping high-entropy alloys with superior mechanical properties via Snoek relaxation.
